title: LLM Agents Grounded in Self-Reports Enable General-Purpose Simulation of Individuals
authors: Park, Zou, Kamphorst, Egan, Shaw, Hill, Cai, Morris, Liang, et al.

blocks.text: AI Simulations Grounded in Rich Self-Reports Increase Accuracy and Reduce Distortion

Abstract: AI simulations of people built from demographic prompts often misjudge individuals and distort sample-level patterns. We test whether rich self-report data reduce these problems. We developed an AI voice interviewer and conducted two-hour interviews following the American Voices Project protocol with 1,052 U.S. adults, who also completed surveys and behavioral experiments. For each participant, we compared simulations prompted with demographic attributes, self-authored personas, survey responses, interview responses, or combined surveys and interviews. We evaluated accuracy on held-out responses, and measured eight statistical distortions at the sample level: biased averages, compressed variance, distorted response distributions, over-correlated items, attitudes collapsing onto one dimension, ideological sorting, amplified experimental effects, and hyper-rationality. On General Social Survey (GSS) items, demographic simulation led to 60.4% accuracy, whereas interview and survey simulation achieved 69.4% and 69.3%, and combining them reached 72.8%, compared with 79.5% for participants’ two-week test–retest agreement. Surveys and interviews also improved prediction of personality traits, but not of incentivized economic choices. Combined interview and survey simulation closed a median of 53.5% of the eight distortion gaps between demographic simulation and participant responses. An open-weight model fine-tuned on other participants’ self-reports and responses to the target questions achieved 75.2% GSS accuracy and closed a median of 69.3% of the distortion gap. Overall, both frontier and fine-tuned models reduced distortions without erasing them, but neither reduced hyper-rationality in economic games. These findings demonstrate that qualitative and quantitative self-reports can improve person-specific simulations and reduce statistical distortions. Significance statement: Can rich portraits of people’s beliefs, attitudes, and life experiences improve AI simulations of those individuals? We used an AI voice interviewer and surveys to collect detailed information from over 1,000 U.S. adults, then compared each person’s answers with simulated responses. Compared with simulations based on demographics alone, simulations using interview and survey data improved predictions about politics, religion, family, and confidence in institutions, as well as personality traits, though not choices in economic games. Combining the two roughly halved seven of eight established statistical distortions, including biased averages, compressed variation, exaggerated relationships among attitudes, and inflated experimental effects. These findings demonstrate the value of grounding AI simulations in people’s own accounts of their lives, and identify distortions that remain.

AI simulation of human attitudes and behavior—leveraging large language models to replicate human responses to social, political, and informational contexts—offers the possibility of a versatile tool for social and behavioral science (1-10). Applications range from piloting measurements or interventions, to understanding how sudden exogenous shocks might impact us prior to the availability of ground truth data, to supporting policy and product development (1, 8, 9, 11-15). Today, these simulations are often built by inputting a demographic profile to a language model, for example age, gender, race, and political orientation, then asking the model to estimate the response a person with that profile would have to a stimulus (2, 16-20).

For these simulations to be useful and trustworthy, they must be accurate at reproducing individuals' attitudes and behavior, and they must not distort population-level statistics. There is already promising evidence that, in some situations, simulation can successfully predict the outcomes of previously unseen interventions (1, 21). However, there is also clear evidence that such success is not universal: in other situations, demographic simulation still suffers from problems with both accuracy and distortion (19, 22-28). Demographic simulation can leave large gaps in individual accuracy (22, 29-31), failing to replicate what the source individuals say or do. Equally concerning, demographic simulation falls prey to a recurring set of statistical distortions: it systematically over- or under-estimates means (19, 22), overly compresses variance (19, 22), excessively correlates responses across variables (19, 33), collapses responses onto too few principal components (33), behave more rationally than people do, a pattern described as hyperrationality (22), agrees more with demographic stereotypes than with the underlying individuals (22, 23, 32), and amplifies experimental effect sizes (1, 7). Together, these shortcomings make it more difficult to determine when, and to what extent, AI simulations of human attitudes and behavior can be deployed.

In this article, we measure the accuracy and levels of distortion observed when constructing AI simulations from rich self-report data such as surveys and interviews. We construct one-to-one AI simulations of 1,052 U.S. adults based on different forms of self-report: demographics, selfauthored brief personas, survey responses, and semi-structured American Voices Project (34) interviews conducted by an AI voice interviewer that we created. Our primary comparisons vary the sources and richness of information supplied to prompted simulations. We also evaluate supervised and fine-tuned approaches (using an open-weight model, Qwen3.5-27B) as benchmarks for performance when labeled responses to the target outcomes are available, and examine whether richer individual information provides leverage under those approaches.

First, to measure accuracy, we compared each approach's simulation response for an individual to the same individual's actual response on the General Social Survey (35, 36), Big Five personality inventory (37), a series of behavioral economic games (38-41), and five published experiments (42-46). Given that participants' own responses may be unstable due to measurement error, respondent uncertainty, drift in the qualities being measured, and other factors yielding survey instability (47), we retest participants on the same measures two weeks later and use their consistency as a benchmark. Second, to measure distortion, we calculated a set of eight measures at the sample level based on distortions noted in the AI simulation literature: mean bias, variance compression, earth mover's distance between answer distributions, mean Spearman's r between item pairs, share of variance on the first principal component across responses, ideological sorting, effect size inflation, and hyper-rationality. We replicated these distortions under demographic simulation, then measured the share of each distortion gap closed by each simulation approach.

Rich self-reports increase accuracy on many of the outcomes. On the General Social Survey, the baseline of demographic simulation achieves 60.4% accuracy at replicating individual responses, compared to participants' own test-retest accuracy, two weeks later, at 79.5%. Populating the simulations with a combination of interview and survey self-reports increases accuracy to 72.8%. Fine-tuning an open-weight LLM, Qwen3.5-27B, with these rich self-reports and supervision on the exact outcomes being predicted further improves accuracy to 75.2%; however, doing so with demographics instead of self-reports largely erases the gain (62.2% accuracy). Rich self-reports also aid prediction of Big Five personality traits: demographic simulation predicts at r = 0.73, compared to combined survey and interview simulation at r = 0.86 and a human test-retest consistency of r = 0.95. However, rich self-reports do not increase accuracy on the incentivized economic games—demographic simulation (MAE = 0.27) and combined survey and interview simulation (MAE = 0.29) perform similarly, benchmarked against a test-retest MAE of 0.21.

Self-reports close a median of 53.5% of the distortion gaps articulated by prior work. Distortions include mean bias (50% of the gap closed [95% CI 49–52]), variance compression (57% ), earth mover's distance between answer distributions (49% ), mean Spearman's r between item pairs (60% ), share of variance on the first principal component (64% ), ideological sorting (60% ), and effect size inflation (46% ). Fine-tuning the LLM on combined interview and surveys further reduces these distortions, closing a median of 69.3% of the gap when given supervision on the outcomes. Surveys and interviews, however, do not reduce the hyper-rationality distortion: across the five economic games, combined simulation does not reliably move the simulations away from rational behavior and toward true human behavior.

In sum, this work examines accuracy and statistical distortions of AI simulation of human behavior across a range of self-report methods. We introduce an AI-guided voice-to-voice interviewer to gather rich self-report data. We contribute the use of test-retest data as a benchmark for aleatory uncertainty in this measurement task. Overall, rich self-reports such as interviews and surveys can often markedly increase accuracy and reduce distortions, opening up pathways for simulation to further improve on these benchmarks.
Using Rich Self-Reports to Create Simulations

We gathered several forms of self-report on individuals, mirroring different methodological traditions in the social and behavioral sciences: demographics, personas, surveys, and interviews. First, self-reported demographics are a common approach leveraged in the simulation literature (2, 16-20). Second, for personas, we asked participants to write a brief paragraph about themselves, including their personal background, personality, and demographic details, similar to material used in prior work (13). Third, structured survey questionnaires provide standardized measures designed to capture the topics social scientists care about, using carefully formulated wording and response categories that support reliable comparison across respondents and, in turn, population-level inference (3, 22, 29, 63). Fourth, we draw on in-depth, semi-structured interviews, which excel at capturing the idiosyncratic factors and lived constraints that shape how people think and act. Semi-structured interviews pair pre-specified prompts with adaptive follow-up questions that respond to participants’ own answers, allowing respondents to foreground what they view as most consequential (48-50). Open-ended narratives can encode multiple features in a single response, linking facts, constraints, and trajectories. By combining pre-specified prompts with responsive probing, interviews expand what can be measured in the first place, not merely how answers are expressed (49, 50).

To scale this semi-structured component, we developed an AI voice interviewer that autonomously conducts in-depth interviews, pairing a fixed protocol with adaptive, real-time follow-up questions to elicit the kind of open-ended narratives that have previously required trained human interviewers (51) (SI Appendix, section 2). To avoid inadvertently tailoring the interview protocol to our evaluation metrics, we sought an existing interview protocol that aimed for broad topical coverage. We adopted the interview protocol developed for the American Voices Project (34). The semi-structured interview protocol included both fixed questions on a wide range of topics from participants’ life stories (e.g., “Tell me the story of your life – from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had”) to their views on current societal issues (e.g., “Some people tell us about experiences of arrest—of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?”; SI Appendix, Table S2), and also follow-up questions generated by the AI interviewer in real-time.

We recruited a quota sample of U.S. adults (N=1,052) to reflect United States adult distributions on age, gender, race, region, education, and party identification (see Materials and Methods). Demographics were obtained from the recruitment panel. For the interview, each participant completed a voice-to-voice interview in English with the AI interviewer, averaging about two hours and producing transcripts with an average length of 6,491 words per participant (std = 2,541; SI Appendix, section 2). The surveys followed the interview: respondents completed the core module of the General Social Survey (GSS; 52), a widely used survey across the social sciences, and the 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI-44; 37), the most commonly used personality battery from psychology. We then elicited participants’ choices in five well-known behavioral economic games with real stakes: the dictator game, the first and second player Trust Games, public goods game, and prisoner’s dilemma (38-41). To ensure genuine engagement, participants were offered monetary incentives on the behavioral economic games. Finally, we collected participants’ choices in five experiments with control and treatment conditions (42-46) drawn from a recent large-scale replication effort (53).
